body.text: 16 October 2020

This page contains data and analysis published by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) from 12 to 16 October 2020. Go to our [live page](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/conditionsanddiseases/articles/coronaviruscovid19roundup/2020-03-26) for the most up-to-date insights on COVID-19.
16 October 2020

body.text: Ethnic background contrasts in deaths involving COVID-19

body.h2: Ethnic background contrasts in deaths involving COVID-19
body.text: A substantial proportion of the [differences in COVID-19 mortality for people of ethnic minority backgrounds](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/birthsdeathsandmarriages/deaths/articles/updatingethniccontrastsindeathsinvolvingthecoronaviruscovid19englandandwales/deathsoccurring2marchto28july2020) can be explained by demographic, geographical and socioeconomic factors, modelling has found.

body.h2: Ethnic background contrasts in deaths involving COVID-19
body.text: After adjustments for those factors, males in all ethnic minority groups other than Chinese retained a higher rate of COVID-19 mortality; for females, all other than Bangladeshi, Chinese and Mixed ethnic groups retained a raised rate of COVID-19 mortality following adjustments.

body.h2: No increase in business closures yet
body.text: No increase in business closures yet

body.h2: No increase in business closures yet
body.text: There was no increase in business closures in Quarter 3 (July to Sept) 2020, according to the [latest data from the Inter-Departmental Business Register (IDBR).](https://www.ons.gov.uk/businessindustryandtrade/business/activitysizeandlocation/bulletins/businessdemographyquarterlyexperimentalstatisticsuk/julytoseptember2020)

body.h2: No increase in business closures yet
body.text: While a higher number of closures might have been expected because of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, business deaths in Quarter 3 were slightly lower than in the same period in 2019 and similar to the number of closures in Quarter 3 of the past three years taken together.

body.h2: No increase in business closures yet
body.text: Notable lags in the removal of a business from the IDBR, because of economic, legal and statistical processes, may explain why business closures have not risen significantly in Quarter 2 (Apr to June) or Quarter 3. Increased business closures as a result of the coronavirus pandemic may yet be reflected in data in subsequent quarters.

body.h2: No increase in business closures yet
body.text: In contrast, the number of business creations in the UK in Quarter 3 2020 was slightly higher than in Quarter 3 2019, following a small fall in Quarter 2 2020. This is somewhat contrary to expectations that business creation would be significantly lower as a result of the coronavirus pandemic.

body.h2: No increase in business closures yet
No increase in business closures yet
body.chartbuilder_h3: Business creations in Quarter 3 2020 were slightly higher than in Quarter 3 2019
body.chartbuilder_h4: Number of businesses added to the Inter-Departmental Business Register (IDBR), quarterly, UK, Quarter 1 (Jan to Mar) 2017 to Quarter 3 (July to Sept) 2020

body.h2: No increase in business closures yet
body.text: There is typically a shorter lag in adding businesses to the IDBR after the effective creation of the business than there is for removing businesses from the IDBR after their effective closure. As such, the rebound in Quarter 3 2020 is likely to reflect a genuine trend for increased business creation.

body.h2: No increase in business closures yet
body.text: The types of businesses created during Quarter 3 2020 were also notably different to the types of businesses created in Quarter 3 in previous years. Broadly speaking, businesses created in this period were smaller than usual (based on both employment and turnover), with businesses created in Quarter 3 having fewer employees on average than in any other quarter in the past four years.

body.h2: No increase in business closures yet
body.text: Industries less affected by the pandemic, including those that offer greater opportunities for homeworking such as professional and administrative services industries, made up a larger share of business births than usual in Quarter 3.

body.h2: UK labour market
body.text: UK labour market

body.h2: UK labour market
body.text: Our [latest figures on the UK labour market](https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/employmentandemployeetypes/bulletins/uklabourmarket/october2020) have now been published.

body.h2: UK labour market
body.text: Early estimates for September 2020 suggest that there is little change in the number of payroll employees in the UK, with an increase of 20,000 compared with August 2020. Since March 2020, the number of payroll employees has fallen by 673,000; however, the larger falls were seen at the start of the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

body.h2: UK labour market
body.text: Data from our Labour Force Survey (LFS) show the employment rate has been decreasing since the start of the coronavirus pandemic, while the unemployment rate and the level of redundancies has been increasing in recent periods. Total hours worked, while still low, show signs of recovering and there are fewer people temporary away from work.

body.h2: UK labour market
UK labour market
body.chartbuilder_h3: Redundancies increased by a record 114,000 on the quarter
body.chartbuilder_h4: UK redundancies, not seasonally adjusted, from June to August, 2005 and June to August, 2020

body.h2: UK labour market
body.text: Redundancies increased by 113,000 on the year, and a record 114,000 on the quarter, to 227,000. The annual increase was the largest since April to June 2009, with the number of redundancies reaching its highest level since May to July 2009.

body.h2: UK labour market
body.text: After a record low of 343,000 vacancies in April to June 2020, there was an increase to 488,000 vacancies in July to September 2020. The level of vacancies is still 40.5% lower than a year ago.

body.h2: UK labour market
body.text: Annual growth in employee pay strengthened in August 2020 as employees continued to return to work from furlough; this followed strong falls in the months since April when growth was affected by lower pay for furloughed employees and reduced bonuses.

body.h2: UK labour market
body.text: The Claimant Count, an [Experimental Statistic](https://www.ons.gov.uk/methodology/methodologytopicsandstatisticalconcepts/guidetoexperimentalstatistics), has increased by 120.3% since March 2020. This includes both those who are working with low income or hours and those who are not working.

body.h2: Productivity measure sees largest fall since 2009
body.text: Productivity measure sees largest fall since 2009

body.h2: Productivity measure sees largest fall since 2009
body.text: Labour productivity, as measured by output per hour, fell by 1.8% in Quarter 2 (Apr to June) 2020. This is the largest fall since Quarter 2 2009. This was driven by a measure of output, gross value added (GVA), falling faster than hours worked. Compared with the previous quarter, GVA fell by 21.5%, while hours worked fell by 20%.

body.h2: Productivity measure sees largest fall since 2009
Productivity measure sees largest fall since 2009
body.chartbuilder_h3: Output per hour fell by 1.8% in Quarter 2 2020, the largest fall since Quarter 2 2009
body.chartbuilder_h4: Labour productivity, as measured by output per hour, Apr to June, 2020.

body.h2: Productivity measure sees largest fall since 2009
body.text: Output per hour and output per worker are usually more closely aligned, but the Coronavirus Job Retention Scheme (CJRS), which allows companies to keep staff employed while working zero hours, has resulted in a large disparity between the two measures, as many furloughed workers are still employed but not producing any output.

body.h2: Productivity measure sees largest fall since 2009
body.text: Further estimates of the effect of the furlough scheme on labour productivity have been explored in our latest [labour productivity bulletin.](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/labourproductivityheadlinemeasuresukapriltojune2020)
